27	## 1 · Defining "agentic engineering" — the title is currently a promise the Intro never quite keeps
28	
29	**What's on the page now:** the Intro's thesis paragraph defines the *practice* in one buried clause ("engineers hand entire features to agents that write, test, and check the code on their own — while the engineer plans the next thing. The practice has a name: agentic engineering"). What it never touches is the *word* — what "agentic" means, where it comes from, why anyone calls it that. And the mechanistic definition ("an LLM with tools, trapped in a loop") doesn't arrive until Era III, four screens later. So a spectator walks three rooms of history holding an undefined title. You're right that it's lacking.
30	
31	**Rubric:** spectator test — the highest-leverage fix available; the title is literally the first jargon on the page. Arena rule — pure copy. Senior tax — zero; seniors enjoy etymology. Companion rule — works cold, and live it hands you a natural opening beat.
32	
33	**The discipline it needs:** the Intro must define the *word*, not the *mechanism*. "An LLM with tools, trapped in a loop" is Era III's punchline — if the Intro explains the loop, room three deflates. The clean split: **Intro says what an agent *is* (something that acts on your behalf, not just answers); Era III shows what an agent *is made of*.** Setup and payoff, same pattern as the search-engine beat.
34	
35	**Where it lands — three options:**
36	
37	**(i) Recommended: a definition card under the H1, styled as a dictionary entry.** The title is a term of art, so define it the way terms of art get defined — dry, mono, editorial. Something in this register:
38	
39	> **agentic** · from *agent* — one who acts.
40	> Software that doesn't just answer. It does things: reads your files, writes code, runs the tests, tries again.
41	>
42	> **agentic engineering** · the practice of planning and directing such agents, rather than typing the code yourself.
43	
44	Placed between the narrator paragraph and the thesis paragraph (or directly under the H1 — dev-server call). The thesis paragraph then sheds its defining clause and gets shorter, which it can afford. The dictionary form is honest about what's happening — you're teaching the room a new word — and it's Pratchett-dry as a form: the joke is that the definition is real.
45	
46	**(ii) Expand the existing thesis paragraph.** One added sentence unpacking "agent" in place. Cheapest, but the paragraph has been carefully pruned three times now and this reverses that work; the definition also stays buried mid-prose where a skimmer misses it.
47	
48	**(iii) Split: plain definition in the Intro, word-origin in Era III's loop deep cut.** Defensible, but you asked for the beginning, and I agree — the title should be legible before the history starts.
49	
50	**A deep-cut candidate that belongs to you specifically:** "agentic" wasn't coined by the AI industry — it's borrowed from psychology. Bandura's social cognitive theory (2001) is built on the "agentic perspective" — humans as intentional actors. And Milgram's obedience work (1974) named the *agentic state*: the condition where a person acts as the instrument of someone else's will and feels responsibility drain away. The AI field picked up the word around 2023 with none of that luggage — but the luggage is the interesting part, because this masterclass's spine is the exact inversion: the machines are the agents now, *and the responsibility conspicuously does not transfer*. "What they write, I still answer for" is the anti-Milgram sentence, already on your page. For a narrator with a cognitive-science degree, that fold writes itself. Honesty rule applies: I'd verify both citations by web search before a word of it ships — say the word and I'll run the verification.

57	
58	**The constraint that shapes everything:** your locked translation model. Live, *you* are the translation — nobody hovers a tooltip while you're talking. The page layer exists for the cold reader (shared link, revisit next month). So whatever we build must be **silent during the talk and available afterwards** — which rules out anything that inflates the prose everyone reads.
59

61	
62	**(A) Recommended: marked terms with tap/hover definitions — the spectator's fold.** A `<Term>` component: jargon gets a subtle dotted underline; tap or hover reveals one plain sentence. `LLM` → *"Large language model — the machine this whole story is about; room one shows you what it really does."* Mirror-image of the senior rail: **▸ folds down for engineers, dotted terms open up for everyone else.** Opt-in, so it costs seniors nothing and the prose stays quiet. Tap one.` — and the two-layer promise becomes literally true on screen.
63

65	
66	**(C) Gloss every term inline in prose.** ("CI — the robot that re-runs every test on every change.") Works for the projected screen, but it bloats copy for everyone, taxes seniors, and undoes three sessions of pruning. No.
67	
68	**(D) A + a take-home.** The `<Term>` dictionary lives in one file (`glossary.ts`: term → plain sentence); the Synthesis (or footer) offers the compiled list as a quiet closing artifact — "every technical word used tonight, in one plain sentence each." 74	3. **One sentence, no metaphor debt.** Plain, not cute. "CI — an automatic checker that re-runs all the tests every time the code changes" — not cake metaphors (arena rule holds even inside a popover).

# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by understanding the current project context, then ask questions one at a time to refine the idea. Once you understand what you're building, present the design and get user approval.

<HARD-GATE>
Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any project, or take any implementation action until you have presented a design and the user has approved it. This applies to EVERY project regardless of perceived simplicity.
</HARD-GATE>

## Anti-Pattern: "This Is Too Simple To Need A Design"

Every project goes through this process. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config change — all of them. "Simple" projects are where unexamined assumptions cause the most wasted work. The design can be short (a few sentences for truly simple projects), but you MUST present it and get approval.

## Checklist

You MUST create a task for each of these items and complete them in order:

1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Offer the visual companion just-in-time** — NOT upfront. The first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than described, offer it then (its own message); on approval its browser tab opens for you. If no visual question ever arises, never offer it. See the Visual Companion section below.
3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
9. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan

## Process Flow

```dot
digraph brainstorming {
    "Explore project context" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions" [shape=box];
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" [shape=box];
    "Present design sections" [shape=box];
    "User approves design?" [shape=diamond];
    "Write design doc" [shape=box];
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" [shape=box];
    "User reviews spec?" [shape=diamond];
    "Invoke writing-plans skill" [shape=doublecircle];

    "Explore project context" -> "Ask clarifying questions";
    "Ask clarifying questions" -> "Propose 2-3 approaches";
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" -> "Present design sections";
    "Present design sections" -> "User approves design?";
    "User approves design?" -> "Present design sections" [label="no, revise"];
    "User approves design?" -> "Write design doc" [label="yes"];
    "Write design doc" -> "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)";
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" -> "User reviews spec?";
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Write design doc" [label="changes requested"];
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Invoke writing-plans skill" [label="approved"];
}
```

**The terminal state is invoking writing-plans.** Do NOT invoke frontend-design, mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. The ONLY skill you invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans.

## The Process

**Understanding the idea:**

- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**

- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why
- YAGNI ruthlessly - remove unnecessary features from every approach and design

**Presenting the design:**

- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

**Design for isolation and clarity:**

- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.

**Working in existing codebases:**

- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.

## After the Design

**Documentation:**

- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
- Commit the design document to git

**Spec Self-Review:**
After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:

1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.

Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.

**User Review Gate:**
After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:

> "Spec written and committed to `<path>`. Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."

Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.

**Implementation:**

- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

## Visual Companion

A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode. Accepting the companion means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.

**Offering the companion (just-in-time):** Do NOT offer it upfront. Wait until a question would genuinely be clearer shown than told — a real mockup / layout / diagram question, not merely a UI *topic*. The first time that happens, offer it then, as its own message:
> "This next part might be easier if I show you — I can put together mockups, diagrams, and comparisons in a browser tab as we go. It's still new and can be token-intensive. Want me to? I'll open it for you."

**This offer MUST be its own message.** Only the offer — no clarifying question, summary, or other content. Wait for the user's response. If they accept, start the server with `--open` so their browser opens to the first screen automatically. If they decline, continue text-only and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per-question decision:** Even after the user accepts, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**

- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions

A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.

If they agree to the companion, read the detailed guide before proceeding:
`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`

The UI should support this linear flow rather than showing everything at once, so the audience discovers each capability as he presents it.

The post-trained mode toggle shouldn't exist until he's established the base model's limitations — it arrives as a reveal, either triggered by an explicit "next" button or automatically after a beat lands. This transforms the demo from an open playground into a staged experience where controls appear progressively.

There's also a visual hierarchy problem: the mode toggle and example toggles look identical (both cyan-bordered pills), but they're fundamentally different kinds of controls. Mode selection is about which era of the model you're interacting with — a core state shift that needs weightier, more distinct visual treatment than example selection.

Reframing the whole thing as a terminal window with chrome solves this: the example selector becomes part of the input area (like a file tab), while the mode becomes a header identity showing the model name and training state. When post-training is revealed, the header transforms into a physical-feeling A/B switch that's visually distinct from the prompt pills.

One approach is a staged reveal inside a single console panel where the title bar initially just shows the base model, examples are small chips in the input area, and after the base model fails on a question, a quiet reveal bar appears below the output offering the next step. Option C adds explicit step control with a button or key to advance through beats, but that risks feeling redundant with the main navigation. I'm leaning toward Option A with maybe a single unlock moment rather than a full sub-stepper. For the example toggles, I should strip away the spoiler language like "watch what happens" — Eric's already doing that live, so the labels just need to describe what's being shown without directing the viewer.

On visibility, I'm thinking both examples should stay visible so the audience sees there's a choice and Eric can jump between them, but the labels need to be neutral. The bigger issue is the layout: having temperature and submit controls below the output feels backwards. The natural flow should be input area with the example chips and submit button, then output below, with observations at the end.

Temperature is really a property of the machine itself—it should live in the header row alongside the model name, like a dial on the device. That also makes the post-training story work physically: when you switch models, the dial disappears. For a live presentation, I need to think about readability from the back of the room too.

There's a tension around those italic observation lines that appear after a run—they're Eric's interpretations, and having them auto-generate might steal his moment as the voice of the work. One gesture per beat: pick prompt → Run → *you talk* → tap → the line confirms you, and the next control appears. Nothing you haven't reached is on screen, and you never have to remember an extra gesture, because the tap is the one you were making anyway.

Three ways to build that:

---

**A · The nameplate becomes a switch** *(recommended)*

One console, staged. It opens as a machine with almost nothing on it: a nameplate reading `davinci-002 · base`, the half-written function already loaded, and `Run ⏎`. No mode control, no second example, no dial — none of that has happened yet.

Each verdict tap opens the next door:

| after | appears |
|---|---|
| the function completes | a second prompt — the selector *materialises* (nothing to confuse it with, since it's the only selector on screen) |
| the question doesn't get answered | the **temperature dial**, in the console's chrome |
| the dial goes strange at 1.4 | a strip under the console: `2022 · humans taught it a format` → **Load the post-trained model →** |

**C · Act cards** — the console announces `Act II · the question` and reconfigures per act. Maximum presenter control, but it puts a second navigation model next to your arrow keys, and it goes back to the page directing the room — which is the thing you just told me not to do.

1. **How many gates?** A as written has four. Four is faithful to "don't show what I haven't reached", but on stage a missed tap means a control that doesn't appear. I'd add insurance: gates never close, and a small muted `show all controls` in the console's corner as a fumble escape. Here's the design. Four sections — veto any of them line by line.

---

## 1 · The stage machine

Five states, each opened by one verdict tap. Gates are monotone (once open, never close). Reload starts fresh; `↺` in the chrome re-arms deliberately.

| stage | on screen | opens when |
|---|---|---|
| **S0 · continuation** | nameplate `davinci-002 · base`, the function prompt already loaded, `Run ⏎`. No selector, no dial, no mode control. | — |
| **S1 · the question** | a *second* prompt appears — the selector materialises, unselected. You tap it, so the turn is yours. | S0 run + tap |
| **S2 · the dial** | temperature enters the chrome | question run in base + tap |
| **S3 · the offer** | strip under the console: `2022 · humans taught it a format` → **Load the post-trained model →** | a run at a band you moved it to (you have to actually turn the dial) + tap |
| **S4 · the flip** | nameplate **becomes** the `base ⇄ post-trained` switch; dial retracts; the same question **auto-runs** and this time gets answered | pressing the offer |

S4 is terminal and free — flip live as often as you like. The dial's rule from then on is simply *visible when the switch says `base`*, which is the story stated as a layout rule.

## 2 · The console

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ davinci-002 · base                 temp ──●── 0.7 steady │  chrome: identity | dial
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ PROMPT   a half-written function   a question            │  body: content
│                                                          │
│ function reverseList(items) {                            │
│   return items.slice().reverse();                        │  prefix in foreground,
│ }                                                        │  completion in cyan
│                                                [Run ⏎]   │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ↩ what just happened                                     │  the transport
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The collision dies because the two controls stop being the same species:

- **Model identity** — in the chrome, and until S4 it isn't a control at all, just a nameplate. At S4 it becomes a **solid slab switch** (active cell filled `bg-foreground`, inactive muted) — reads as hardware, one of two, physical.
- **Prompts** — in the body, no borders, no pills: mono text with a cyan underline on the active one. That's the same "underline = you are here" grammar the stepper now speaks, so it costs the audience no new vocabulary.

Projection: output goes from `text-sm` to ~`15px/leading-7`, controls up one notch from `text-xs`. Cyan stays strictly on *machine output* and active-state marks — no cyan prose anywhere in the demo, per the senior-rail ruling. The verdict affordance uses `↩`, **not** `▸` — that glyph is spoken for.

## 3 · Copy consequences

- Prompt labels lose their stage directions: `A question (watch what happens)` → **`a question`**. That parenthesis was your line.
- The demo's opening italic — *"Most of the world met these models believing they're a search engine with better manners. Try it — ask it a question."* — I want to **cut it**. It directs the room, and at S0 it points at a question that isn't loaded yet. The era paragraph above already frames the room; the search-engine belief is a thing you say better than the page does. (Your call — the alternative is demoting it to a dry console caption.)
- Verdicts become keyed by `(prompt, mode, band)` so the dial beat gets its own line at high temperature — the *"how do I reverse time? who is asking?"* continuation earns more than the generic "it's continuing your pattern".
- One new mono whisper when the dial arrives. Draft: `temperature — how much the dice get to decide`.

## 4 · Code shape

`index.tsx` is 175 lines with four near-duplicate verdict blocks inline; this change would push it past 300. So it splits:

- **`stage.ts`** — `Stage`, `advance(stage, event)`, visibility predicates. Pure, TDD.
- **`verdicts.ts`** — `verdictFor({ promptId, mode, band })`. Pure, TDD. Kills the four inline conditionals.
- **`console-chrome.tsx`** — nameplate → switch, dial, `↺`.
- **`index.tsx`** — orchestration and streaming only.
- **`session-store.ts`** — module-level stage that survives step navigation and dies on reload.

`selector.ts` / `completions.ts` change only in label copy; their existing tests keep passing.

---

Does this hold? Three things I'd especially like a yes/no on: **cutting the opening italic**, **the S3 gate requiring you to actually move the dial** (faithful, but it means a tap at the default temperature won't open the offer), and **the auto-run on flip**.

**Date:** 2026-07-24 · **Amends:** `2026-07-15-masterclass-agentic-engineering-rework-design.md` · **Event:** 2026-07-28

`post-trained`) and a prompt row rendered in the *same* pill treatment, both live
from the first second, with the temperature dial and Submit stranded below the
output. Two problems follow.

**The controls collide.** "Which machine am I talking to" and "what am I feeding
it" are different species of decision wearing the same clothes.

**The room is spoiled.** Post-training is the room's payoff — the ChatGPT moment.
Sitting on screen from the start, it announces the ending before the story begins.

This redesign rebuilds the demo as a **staged console** that reveals itself one
beat at a time, in the order the presenter actually walks.

## The presentation frame

Two rules govern everything below.

1. **Nothing is on screen that the presenter hasn't reached.** Confirmed beat
   order: continuation → the question → the dial → the flip. The dial beat is
   always performed.
2. **The page does not speak first.** Verdict lines no longer appear on their own
   when a run finishes. Eric says the line; then he taps, and the page agrees with
   him. Cold readers tap it themselves, so the exhibit still works from a shared
   link with nobody narrating.

transport control.** One gesture per beat — pick prompt → `Run` → talk → tap —
and the tap both prints the confirmation and opens the next door. No extra
gesture to remember on stage.

The affordance appears under the output only once streaming has finished, and is
replaced in place by the verdict line when tapped. The next `Run` clears the
verdict and re-arms the affordance.

Five stages. Gates are monotone — once open, never closed. A page reload starts
fresh; a `↺` in the console chrome re-arms deliberately. The revealed stage lives
in a module-level session store so stepping to Era II and back does **not**
re-lock the demo.

|---|---|---|
| **S0 · continuation** | nameplate `davinci-002 · base`, the half-written function already loaded, `Run ⏎`. No prompt selector, no dial, no mode control. | — |
| **S1 · the question** | a second prompt appears; the selector materialises, with the question **unselected** so the turn to it is the presenter's | S0 run completes + verdict tap |
| **S2 · the dial** | temperature enters the console chrome | question run in base mode + verdict tap |

| **S4 · the flip** | the nameplate **becomes** a `base ⇄ post-trained` switch; the dial retracts; the same question **auto-runs** and is answered | pressing the offer |

live as often as the room needs. The dial's rule from S4 onward is simply
*visible when the switch reads `base`* — the story restated as a layout rule.

**Why the S3 gate requires a real dial move:** the beat is "the same prompt goes
strange." Opening the offer on a tap at the default temperature would put the
payoff on screen while the presenter is still mid-beat. Accepted cost: a run at
the opening band does not advance the stage.

question it just failed, in place, with no further gesture. That is the ChatGPT
moment compressed into one press.

├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ PROMPT   a half-written function   a question            │  body: content
│                                                          │

- **Model identity** lives in the chrome. Until S4 it is not a control at all —
  a mono nameplate, no border, nothing to click, so nobody hunts for a second
  mode. At S4 it becomes a **solid slab switch**: two cells on a muted track,
  active cell filled (`bg-foreground` / `text-background`), inactive muted. It
  reads as hardware — one of two, physical.

  uppercase mono `prompt` label. No borders, no pills: mono text, the active one
  carrying a cyan underline. That is the same "underline = you are here" grammar
  the stepper header now speaks, so it costs the audience no new vocabulary.

a dependency). No bounce.

Cyan stays on **machine output** (the streamed completion) and active-state marks
only. No cyan prose line anywhere in the demo — cyan prose belongs to the
engineers' register (`//` asides, field-note rules) per the ruling in `eb9721b`.
